opus-5.5.text:
Every explanation of a sensory map is a simplification, and I try to be honest that I'm making one.

When I talk about color, I'll say something like "there's a map where red sits here, green there, blue over there, and every color you can see has an address." That's a useful story, and it's broadly true. But it hides a lot: the nonlinearities in how cones respond, how context and adaptation shift what you perceive, and the fact that the "map" is really a convenient coordinate system we impose rather than something sitting in your head.

With smell it's even more pronounced. When we describe a principal odor map, I'll often say "molecules that smell similar end up close together, and molecules that smell different end up far apart." That's the core idea, and it's what makes the map useful for prediction. But underneath that sentence are many caveats. Odor perception depends on concentration, so a molecule can smell quite different when it's faint than when it's strong. Mixtures don't behave like simple averages of their parts. People differ genetically in their olfactory receptors, so my map isn't exactly your map. And the descriptors we train on, words like "fruity," "woody," or "musky," are a lossy human vocabulary laid over something much richer.

So I think of the simplifications as scaffolding. They help someone build intuition, and you need that intuition before the caveats make any sense. If I opened with "here are the fourteen ways this breaks," nobody would understand what was breaking. The risk is when the scaffolding gets mistaken for the building, when people hear "map of smell" and assume we've solved olfaction. We haven't. We have a representation that captures a meaningful amount of structure, and it does a good job predicting what people will say a single molecule smells like at a typical concentration. That's real progress, and it's also a narrow slice of the whole problem.

My rule of thumb is to simplify in a direction that's true, so that when someone learns more, they're refining their picture rather than having to throw it out. A good simplification should be the first term in a series expansion, not a different function altogether.

r001.rationale: The response describes a color map as a useful coordinate system, but does not say that different color-space maps can be translated into one another.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I'm always a little bit careful here, because the honest answer is that the map I draw on a whiteboard is a cartoon, and I know it's a cartoon. When I say the retina is a map, that's basically true. There's a sheet of photoreceptors, light lands on it, there's a spatial grid, and that spatial grid gets more or less preserved as you go up into visual cortex. For hearing, the cochlea unrolls frequency along a length, low to high, so you get a tonotopic map, and again that's a simplification, but it's a pretty good one.

Where I get more uncomfortable is when I then say, "and smell doesn't have a map," because that's a little bit of a rhetorical move. What I actually mean is that there's no obvious low-dimensional axis in the physical world that the olfactory system is laid out along. Wavelength and frequency are one number. A molecule is not one number. It's a shape, a charge distribution, a bunch of functional groups, and the receptors in your nose, on the order of four hundred types in humans, each respond to overlapping and weird subsets of those molecules. So the "map" that exists in the olfactory bulb is a map of receptor identity, not of some property of the stimulus we can write down. That's a real difference, and I think it's the interesting one, but if I compress it to "vision has a map and olfaction doesn't," I've thrown away some nuance that people who actually work on the bulb would rightly object to.

So the way I think about it is, every simplification I make should be one I could unpack on demand. If someone pushes on it, I want to be able to say, here's the fuller picture, here's where the cartoon breaks, and here's why the cartoon was still the right thing to say first. The thing I try hard not to do is simplify in a way that points in the wrong direction. Saying "smell is unstructured" would be wrong. Saying "smell is structured, but we didn't know what the structure was, and we had to learn it from data rather than read it off the physics" is what I actually believe, and that's really the whole motivation for why we went and built models to find that structure in the first place.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses spatial, tonotopic, and olfactory maps, but does not state that different color-space maps can be translated into one another.

astra-6.text: I think of them as useful approximations. When we talk about a sensory map, it’s tempting to imagine a neat picture where every sensation has a location, and nearby things feel similar. That’s a helpful starting point, but it leaves out a lot: context, experience, and what the brain is trying to do with that information. So the question for me is whether the simplification preserves the structure we need to answer a particular question. If it does, it’s useful. If we start mistaking it for the whole story, it becomes a problem.

Does it help us make a prediction or design an experiment? If it does, it’s useful, even if it isn’t the whole story.
